article.title: Beyond Plantation Capitalism
article.author: Dick Price, Sharon Kyle, Peter Laarman
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. An interview with Rev. Peter Laarman by Dick Price and Sharon Kyle What will it take to dismantle an economic system that concentrates extraordinary wealth in the hands of a tiny elite while millions of working people struggle to survive? And how do we build a movement capable of changing not only the policies that sustain inequality but also the values that make such inequality seem acceptable? These questions were at the center of a recent LA Progressive conversation with Rev. Peter Laarman, a retired minister who formerly led Progressive Christians Uniting in Los Angeles. A member of the National Council of Elders, Laarman also serves on its King and Breaking Silence team. Speaking with LA Progressive co-founders Dick Price and Sharon Kyle about his article, Curbing Cancerous Capitalism: An Organizing Challenge for the Ages , Laarman explored the enduring influence of racial hierarchy, the economic legacy of slavery, and the challenge of building a movement that confronts both. Plantation Capitalism (27:12) The Legacy of Plantation Capitalism Central to Laarman's argument is a phrase frequently invoked by the late Rev. James Lawson Jr., the legendary civil rights strategist and advocate of radical nonviolence: "plantation capitalism." Laarman knew Lawson through their overlapping work in Los Angeles, including labor organizing and economic justice initiatives. Lawson had been instrumental in the Justice for Janitors campaign and Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice, helping connect struggles for workers' rights with a broader movement for social transformation. For Lawson, plantation capitalism was not simply a reference to the historical plantation economy. It described an enduring relationship between concentrated economic power and the people whose labor generates wealth. "The real point," Laarman explained, "is the default wage for most of the history of people on this continent was zero," referring to the uncompensated labor imposed through chattel slavery. He argued that the assumption among powerful interests that labor should cost as little as possible never disappeared with emancipation. Kyle connected that observation to contemporary wage labor, noting that although chattel slavery and wage employment are fundamentally different legal arrangements, both raise questions about who controls the wealth produced by workers. Laarman agreed that wage labor is inherently extractive under capitalism, pointing to the growing concentration of economic power. The conversation turned to the industrial transformation that accompanied the Civil War era. Laarman described how skilled workers in the 1840s and 1850s valued their independence and feared that emerging factory systems would strip them of economic autonomy. He also emphasized that opposition to slavery's expansion did not necessarily translate into support for Black equality. Related: Marlon James Uncovers Depths of Depravity in Evangelical Christianity The Two Walls That Defeated Reconstruction Laarman identified two major forces that undermined the promise of Reconstruction. The first was white racial resentment, particularly resistance to repairing the enormous harm inflicted through slavery. The second was Wall Street's determination to industrialize the nation and exploit its resources following the Civil War. Many northern industrialists who had supported abolition were nevertheless unwilling to support meaningful economic restitution for formerly enslaved people. Instead, Laarman argued, they accepted the continuing racial caste system because it served the interests of industrial capitalism. That history reveals a distinction too often obscured in American accounts of emancipation: ending the legal ownership of human beings did not end the struggle over who controlled labor, property, and the wealth labor produced. Kyle drew a connection between that history and today's extraordinary concentrations of private wealth, questioning why the economic contributions of millions of workers are so routinely attributed to a handful of billionaires. Electoral Victories Are Not Enough The discussion then moved from history to the political challenges confronting the United States today. Laarman warned against assuming that Democratic electoral victories, however welcome, would produce the fundamental changes required to confront inequality and racial domination. Even a sweeping Democratic victory, he suggested, could encourage complacency among comfortable constituencies. He worried that political leaders might leave intact extraordinary executive powers, expansive immigration enforcement structures, and the economic arrangements that direct wealth upward. The danger, he argued, is that temporary political relief could substitute for lasting structural change. "I firmly believe that a transformed politics has to follow a transformed culture," Laarman said, describing the work ahead as both a spiritual and psychological challenge. But he rejected the notion that people should wait for some sweeping moral awakening before acting. Immediate resistance remains essential, particularly in defending vulnerable communities, building mutual aid networks, and exposing the influence of wealthy political donors. Related: Chattel Slavery vs. Wage Labor: Who Is Really Free? The Search for a Different Kind of Movement Kyle pressed Laarman on a question that has become increasingly urgent for those who recognize the depth of America's problems: Where are the organizations that understand the structural nature of economic and racial domination and are actually developing ways to overcome it? Laarman acknowledged that the answer remains incomplete. He described emerging initiatives seeking to connect organizers, abolitionist movements, and communities committed to social transformation. Within the National Council of Elders, he said, discussions are underway about developing local "begin-again circles." These gatherings would offer activists something different from another meeting, campaign, or organizational obligation. They would provide spaces for reflection, renewal, trust, and meaningful connection. Laarman envisioned places where participants could be vulnerable, where everyone would be heard, and where spiritual nourishment would not depend on religious affiliation. Such spaces, he suggested, could help sustain people engaged in exhausting struggles against entrenched power. He also pointed to historical moments when profound cultural changes accompanied political transformation, including the struggles in Poland, Czechoslovakia, and South Africa. Although no example guarantees a lasting transformation, these experiences demonstrate that deeply established systems of domination are not necessarily permanent. Challenging the Wealthy to See Their Common Interests Price raised another formidable obstacle: America's affluent professional and business classes, many of whom benefit substantially from the existing system. Laarman acknowledged that this group represents an important political constituency whose members frequently identify with billionaires rather than working people. Yet he argued that smaller business owners and millionaires are increasingly vulnerable to the same concentrations of economic power, particularly through private equity and emerging technologies. The organizing challenge is to persuade them that their interests are not necessarily aligned with those of the ultrawealthy. That may prove difficult in a culture that encourages people to imagine themselves as future billionaires, even when the economic system makes such outcomes extraordinarily unlikely. Related: Recalling the Torments of a Radical Truthteller Reaching for a Higher Plane Throughout the conversation, Laarman returned to Lawson's conviction that economic justice cannot be separated from the moral and spiritual condition of society. His argument was not that political organizing should give way to religious reflection. Rather, the two must reinforce each other. Movements need practical strategies, durable institutions, and the power to resist exploitation. But they also need a shared understanding of human dignity strong enough to challenge a culture that treats unlimited accumulation as an unquestioned virtue. For Laarman, the task is neither to dismiss existing movements nor to wait for a perfect new organization to appear. It is to connect struggles already underway while inviting participants to imagine a more profound transformation. "We're gonna reach higher," he said. "We're not gonna piss on other people's efforts, but we're going to invite people to step up to a higher plane." The challenge raised by Lawson's concept of plantation capitalism remains: Can Americans build an economy in which the people who create society's wealth also share meaningfully in its benefits and exercise power over the conditions of their lives? Laarman does not pretend to have a complete blueprint. But his insistence that structural change must be accompanied by cultural transformation offers a direction for those determined to move beyond simply managing an unjust system. The task is not merely to curb capitalism's most destructive excesses. It is to organize a society in which human dignity matters more than the unchecked accumulation of wealth.
